# The Parasitic Draw Mystery on a 2010 Kia Optima

When you connect jumper cables to a dead battery, the alternator and the donor vehicle share the electrical load. The engine runs because the alternator is actively charging the starter motor and powering the ECU, fuel pump, and ignition coils. However, the moment you remove those cables and disconnect the boost source, the car dies immediately. This specific behavior on a 2010 Kia Optima usually points to one of two distinct failure modes: a failing alternator or a parasitic drain that was masked by the jumper's current but becomes critical once the donor vehicle is removed.

The most common culprit in this scenario is an alternator that has lost its ability to generate sufficient voltage under load. While the battery might show 12.4V or higher while parked, it often sits right at the edge of collapse when the engine runs but the alternator isn't pushing enough amps. When you are jumpered, the donor vehicle supplies the missing current, allowing the car to idle and eventually shut down smoothly because the alternator is effectively bypassed. Once the cables are removed, the alternator must immediately pick up the slack for the entire electrical system. If its internal diode rectifier is shorted or the voltage regulator has degraded, the output drops below the threshold required to keep the ECU alive, causing an immediate stall.

To diagnose this without immediately replacing parts, you need a multimeter and a methodical load test. Start with the engine running on battery power alone (once the car restarts after jumper removal). Measure the voltage at the battery terminals while idling. On a healthy system, you should see between 13.8V and 14.4V. If the reading hovers around 12.6V or lower while the engine is running, the alternator is not charging. This confirms the alternator is the weak link that the jumper cables were temporarily compensating for.

However, there is a second possibility specific to older vehicles like the 2010 Optima: a parasitic drain exacerbated by the removal of the jumper. When you have jumper cables connected, the voltage at the terminals is held artificially high by the donor car. If you have a component stuck in the "on" positionâsuch as a faulty interior light relay, an aftermarket alarm module, or a failing body control moduleâit draws current continuously. While the jumper is attached, the battery voltage stays stable because the external source replenishes what the bad component steals. Once the jumper is removed, if the battery was already marginal (common in cars sitting for long periods), that single parasitic load can drain the remaining capacity instantly, causing the ECU to reset and the engine to die.

To distinguish between these two issues, perform a voltage drop test on the alternator output wire while the engine is running. If you find the alternator is outputting correctly but the car still dies upon cable removal, your focus must shift to the battery health and potential internal shorts in the fuse box. It is also worth checking the battery terminals for corrosion or loose connections that increase resistance; high resistance can mimic a charging failure by causing voltage sag under load.

In many cases involving this specific model year, the issue resolves itself once the battery is fully recharged and the alternator is confirmed to be holding stable voltage above 13.5V at idle. If the alternator checks out but the car still dies immediately after disconnecting the jumper, inspect all fuses related to accessories that might remain active when the key is off. A simple multimeter check across any fuse while the ignition is off can reveal a short circuit drawing excessive amps, which would explain why the battery voltage collapses as soon as the external power source is severed.
